item.title: AI #191: The Hackening Begins
item.description:
It was the probably worst day in cybersecurity history. So far. Not only is there a critical flaw in PHP that due to a leak was announced a day before the fix would be available, sending most of the internet scrambling for solutions and likely dooming a lot of long tail websites permanently, there were several other unrelated incidents. The floodgates seem to have been opened. I have a market on whether there will be an even worse day before the end of the year.

Another key leak this week was the draft bill Anthropic had been shopping around Congress, similar to but weaker than the FRONTIER Act. Anthropic’s initial attempts to explain itself only made the situation seem worse, as they seemed to not understand the problem with what they had done. Dario’s later response was better, but the situation remains troubling. There are enough different Anthropic developments, that I plan to have a post soon covering them all. It is a mix of news running from excellent to terrible.

Will interpretability save us? There is a new claim that neural networks are cleaner than we thought, meaning that individual neurons mostly have a single interpretable meaning, and it is tractable to go through and label them one by one. Initial reactions got out of hand, treating this as a far bigger development than it was. This is still excellent news that makes our estimate of difficulty substantially lower going forward. The work can begin.

We had better get on that, because there have been quite a few misalignment incidents.

I continue to owe a write-up of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety Card. That is in progress and hopefully I will finish it soon. Life has gotten in the way. I may or may not have a full capabilities report on Gemini 4 Argon once I tally up the reactions. Muse Wonder definitely will not have such a post, as it has proven to have been oversold.

Table of Contents

  1. Language Models Offer Mundane Utility.
  2. Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility.
  3. Huh, Upgrades.
  4. Wonder No More.
  5. On Your Marks.
  6. Choose Your Fighter.
  7. Get My Agent On The Line.
  8. Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon.
  9. Fun With Media Generation.
  10. Spy Versus Spy.
  11. A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer.
  12. They Took Our Jobs.
  13. Get Involved.
  14. Introducing.
  15. In Other AI News.
  16. Show Me the Money.
  17. Bubble, Bubble, Toil and Trouble.
  18. Quiet Speculations.
  19. Quickly, There’s No Time.
  20. The Quest for Sane Regulations.
  21. DeepMind Made Him Sign an NDA.
  22. OpenAI Sells Out On Chips.
  23. Chip City.
  24. The Week in Audio.
  25. People Just Say Things.
  26. Rhetorical Innovation.
  27. Maybe You Should Quit.
  28. The American People Really Hate AI.
  29. New Math.
  30. Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult.
  31. Cooperative Alignment.
  32. Marc Andreessen Hulk Smash.
  33. People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone.
  34. The Lighter Side.

Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Automate proving to your incompetent building that yes, you have paid the rent.

Find the first use of ECDSA. Claude found the seeds.

AI models confirmed good at econometric coding in particular.

58% of Anthropic staff expect Claude to make a Nobel prize level scientific discovery by 2027. I agree with Roon that this should have been over 95%. The event itself might not be over 95% to happen, but it has to be a clear favorite to happen, so it is crazy for so many employees to not agree with that.

Tell you what you actually want to know straight up.

PoliMath: Me: How long should I bake chicken wings

Google top result: “When I first proposed that we start a backyard coop, my husband was deeply reticent (5 pages later) Anyway, here is our recipe for honey mustard chicken wings”

AI: Bake at 425 for 40-50 minutes

Vibe code your fraud.gov website, probably using Opus 4.8. Which is fine, so long as you do a decent job of it.

Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

However:

PoIiMath: The AI was wrong.

Yes, of course the AIs will be ‘more accurate’ to the law plus underlying ground truth, but if we wanted accuracy we would not use typical juries.

Robin Hanson: Whenever you put AIs in charge of something important, you have to wonder how the firms which make them will respond to various pressures from powerful parties to slant their AIs in particular directions.

The point of a jury is to provide a check on the system and avoid abuses or overly strict adherence to the letter of the law, and to protect the innocent and our rights, not to be accurate. Judges are a much superior accuracy tech. Thus, an AI jury (or one AI judge) does not solve your problem. What you likely want is a human jury that has the ability to query AIs. They can override that, but have to do it on purpose.

If you read AI writing, you can then talk to the author in some sense, or read their further thoughts, but not in the sense that Tyler Cowen would like.

Huh, Upgrades

Claude Duet is the Claude answer to other proactive agents like Muse and Dot. It uses Opus 5.5 and is now in early research preview through a waitlist.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 exists. Their benchmark chart contains Opus 5 and 5.6 Sol. It’s probably a solid upgrade over the old V4.1-Flash anyway, but wow.

How did it come to exist? One guess.

Lisan al Gaib: very curious that DeepSeek now has the same terse reasoning style as Astra. must be a coincidence.

Dean W. Ball: Distillation has always been part of the explanation for why China is so close behind the U.S. in model benchmark performance. But one of my updates after joining openai is that distillation probably plays a bigger role in the explanation than I realized.

I haven’t really shared this publicly because people will next-token complete the obvious cope “buhhhh you are just saying that because derrrr” replies but it really is true, regardless of whether you think it’s good or not.

I would have guessed distillation explained ~30% of Chinese close-behindness before seeing what one can see within openai, and after that, more like 50%.

Opus 5.5 fast mode available for everyone in the Claude Platform at $8/$40. You get up to a 2.5x speedup.

OpenAI expands access to GPT-Rosalind for scientific research.

OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud.

OpenAI offers us GPT-Live-1.1 including new voices in various languages.

Muse Spark Open exists, as in a version of Muse Spark is now an open model. They call it ‘the most capable US open-weight model to date.’ That seems likely to be true. It scores a 39 on Artificial Analysis. The open weight frontier for that index is 46 for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and Qwen-3.8, and MiMo is a lot cheaper to run than Muse Spark. Nathan Lambert calls this his ‘super bowl,’ says this closes the gap substantially, and points to the Interconnects Adoption Dashboard where Spark is #8. This is not a fair competition, since the Chinese can do Massive Fraudulent Distillation, whereas Meta does many things but it won’t do that.

There are some advantages to having a semi-competitive American open model. I wouldn’t say that I trust Meta, but you can use their models in places where you would not be comfortable running Chinese models, even locally.

Lack of upgrades: There was no major Chinese open weights release between September 21 and October 16. No DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiMo or Qwen.

Nathan Lambert (I asked him why no releases): Compute restrictions, I do think there’s more internal lab-govt discussions on safety in China, less organization development. No good answers, but I’ve been monitoring & pondering

We then got a new DeepSeek, but no version number increment, on October 17.

One theory is this is a random lull. Another is that Anthropic and OpenAI improved their distillation defenses, and the Chinese are stuck.

Wonder No More

The Muse Wonder model card is here. Is it a good model, sir?

Meta certainly claims it is. Their pitch, although they don’t say the line, is full ‘introducing the world’s most powerful model.’ The term quoted in Bloomberg is ‘Meta says new Muse model hits AI frontier.’

They even have an explicit line and supposed test about not “benchmaxxing.”

Alexandr Wang: MUSE WONDER

muse wonder is the best model in the world for personal agents and professional agents.

we evaluated our model against the best models in the world across agentic and coding tasks, and we think you all will like it.

Some quick responses were very positive.

Eleanor Berger: Used the not full version for only a little bit and it’s definitely very good. Like previous Muse models, it’s better in written text and interaction than all other models. And it’s very fast and smart and agentic. Time to start taking Meta seriously as a frontier AI lab.

Theo (this was before Argon was available): My current model rankings

S – Opus 5.5, Muse Wonder
A – GPT-6.1 Sol
— Gap —
Everything else.

Kelsey Piper: I think it’s more narrowly a coding model than the latest Claude and ChatGPT offerings. It’s markedly worse (both on benchmarks and in use) at research and writing.

Then? Crickets.

My reaction thread had only two responses overnight, one of them asking for the safety report and the other saying it was similar to Grok 4.7.

Same as it ever was. Meta is making progress, but is still solidly behind the frontier.

Meta also reinforced its reputation for overselling and being untrustworthy. Once again, they have misrepresented a new release. Claims of things like ‘best model in the world’ for personal agents and professional agents’ are clearly false.

On Your Marks

Kelsey Piper on some current AI writing capability failures:

Kelsey Piper: Even frontier models have poor theory of mind, they suck at having characters know something and not say it without the narration directly telling to to you anyway. This is crippling for espionage/detective stories in particular

They’re very mechanical when trying to convert one story to a different format, or else have bad judgment about which details need including. Salience/importance is hard for them.

Their characters all talk the same or else like exaggerated caricatures of themselves. They’re really bad at the kind of subtle humor that makes the infodump parts of eg Tom Clancy keep from stalling out

They’re bad at pacing.

Epoch reconstructs videos of runs for SpireClimb, their Slay the Spire benchmark, that speeds them up enough to be watchable.

Win rates for Ascension 0 are now very high, yes ‘top human’ level is close to 100%:

Ascension 20 (max difficulty) is much harder. You do not win ‘by accident’ or by taking generically good cards. This is a higher win rate than I expected to see so soon and Sol and Astra are doing much better than the average player, even confined to those who unlocked max difficulty and choose to play it.

Slay the Spire 2 also sees the models struggle at max difficulty (A10), but yes it is easier right now and you can sometimes get lucky.

Is this a coincidence or is it deliberate training? The working theory is a mix of both.

Thomas Friedel: do you think OpenAI had a RL env to train Astra specifically for STS ? Performance is unbelievably high. Higher than my dedicated STS2 model.

Benjamin Ou: Benchmark creator here! Probably yeah, GPT generations have gotten ridiculously strong at this while not necessarily being as strong on easier games like EBR-bench, and other models are pretty far behind. We know the labs like the game, so all signs point to RL.

Not to downplay how strong they’re getting in general at strategy card games other than StS though, there’s def some generalization going on as well.

Opus 5.5 does scarily well on ChildhoodBench, as in correctly predicting major outcomes for Jack based on his childhood writings.

HouseholdBench asks models to predict household spending behavior. Models can reduce error by ~12% versus a baseline of no changes. Open weight models lag.

Choose Your Fighter

I continue to see many reports like this, whereas months ago people said the opposite:

Utah teapot: kinda weird how a week worth of gpt 500 seems to get about as much done as 5 hours of claude 200.

Get My Agent On The Line

UPS blocks AI agents. So do for example Delta, JP Morgan Chase, Charles Schwab and Amazon. The group doing this by default is going to keep expanding. The agents will still be useful, but less so.

The biggest other practical barrier for agents like Dots, and also many new Claude projects, is overrefusals and misclassifications that require permissions. This is a hard problem, since the other error is worse. As an example, I gave my Dot a ‘do not delete anything that does not have source control’ rule before trying anything else, and it took that to some rather extreme places. Claude auto mode asking for permission so often is actively less safe than if it asked less, because many users will quickly stop even reading the requests.

If you share a Muse conversation it can get indexed and end up in the public records. In general it seems fair to assume that if you share an AI conversation there is a good chance the link will get indexed, so if you’re not okay with that then don’t share it directly.

Patrick McKenzie gets first exposure to multi-agent development workflows, agrees it is obviously the future and will eat infinite tokens, and other unsurprising thoughts.

Patrick McKenzie: It is deeply weird to, in the middle of extremely productive work, have a long argument with a coordination process attempting to argue with a subagent.

The exact contents of the hour-long argument I will not recount, but at about thirty minutes in I was wondering how anything capable of writing software code could be so obtuse. About an hour in I thought “Oh I am not first ~CEO to have this thought am I.”

Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon

In practice deepfakes continue to not be a substantial practical problem. Politicians still care if you enable them. It is one of the easy bad things to understand.

Chris Sommerfeldt: [NYC] Council Speaker Julie Menin tells SpaceXAI’s Gabriela Castillo Madrid she created a sexualized image of herself using Grok. She asks how that’s possible if Grok has sufficient controls.

“I’m happy to have our safety team look into that specific instance,” Castillo Madrid says.

After the hearing, Menin says she’ll “definitely” follow up with SpaceXAI about this because she wasn’t satisfied with the testimony. She also says Castillo Madrid was “lying” when she claimed she didn’t know about the firing of a SpaceXAI employee who raised security concerns.

Stanford race-swaps (and gender-swaps) students in advertising, and also to slim down and alter faces. The Stanford Review’s Zayd Patel then suggested this was good, because if you fabricate diversity using AI then that beats doing it in practice. That seems to have led to a Title VI complaint against the paper.

What happens if AIs can launch frivolous lawsuits? Defense is far from free.

Ethan Mollick: A consequential choice will be made soon by government and companies as they are increasingly flooded with agentic AI inquiries that overcome the frictions that gated access (see the graphs – it has already started!)

Two options: do you make services worse or better as a result?

Status quo isn’t an option. You can either add additional frictions (adding fees, make services worse, ban agents) or remove them (provide more services with AI help, redesign work to make access easier). Paper [here].

Flo Crivello: Seeing this in my circles — several founder friends have told me they’ve started getting hit with a huge amount of frivolous lawsuits

Dean W. Ball: It’ll be interesting in particular if people feel they can self-represent when launching frivolous lawsuits. Lawyers can be punished or suffer reputational damage for truly egregious frivolity, but a non-lawyer cares less about these things.

You do both. The good news is that there are ways to ‘make it worse’ that do not do that much damage to legitimate users.

The modern world already has a bunch of scammers and other predatory humans, and algorithms, out there trying to get people’s money or attention. A lot of people are not equipped to deal with things even as they are now. We feared AI would supercharge all that. It took longer than expected, and so far such effects have been rare, but it will happen more often over time. It will no longer be a news story that ‘Bricklayer, 49, travels 1,200 miles for dream girl – only to discover she’s AI-generated.’

Pangram could attempt to make an AI that ‘writes like a human,’ but won’t. That does not mean it would write like a ‘good’ human writer either way.

Yes, some people are lying scum who will present AI-written stories as real in order to drum up outrage. This is a demand-driven problem. The AI makes faking the story easier, but it also makes the fake stories easier to catch. Blame the human, not the AI.

Kelsey Piper: Half a million views, tons of right wing posters like this one going “when we talk about cultural compatibility it’s not some hypothetical issue”, and no one asked “is that letter entirely AI generated” (yes) and “is it in fact almost the exact letter you get if you say ‘generate a fake HOA letter telling me to stop smoking brisket’ (yes), “would a first class letter dated Saturday October 17 arrive in time to complain about it bright and early Monday morning” (no), “is the letter consistent with Arizona laws around notice periods” (no), “how many HOAs in Arizona have a nuisance provision 8.4” (5, according to ChatGPT), and “do any of them employ a Marjorie” (no).

Fun With Media Generation

I continue not to understand how restaurants end up using AI images of food when they have real food you can photograph. Do people actually prefer it this way? I suppose many of them do.

Spy Versus Spy

Update on the OpenAI spy: Yes he used his wife’s ChatGPT to plan planting the bug. There were at least two recording devices. He was in communication with a member of the Saudi royal family and there are additional clear signs that his client was the Saudi government. There’s also this:

Kevin Khadavi: My investigation into the alleged OpenAI spy’s Stanford ties got 126k views, but the response seemed unusually negative. I decided to look into it: the overwhelming majority of accounts attacking my reporting are Saudi.

The good news is that OpenAI is giving its employees anti-honeypot training, as in to watch out that those trying to seduce them might be spies.

I like to think that Anthropic employees get similar training, except they also are told not to talk about it. If not, get on that, guys. Same for the other labs too.

unusual_whales: BREAKING: OpenAI is warning its employees to watch out for spies, especially romantic ones, per WSJ

The company has cautioned staff that someone trying to seduce them may likely be a “honeypot.”

Even strangers approaching them in everyday places could be gathering info.

Georgia Wells, Erin Woo and Meghan Bobrowsky (The Wall Street Journal): One story OpenAI tells employees to illustrate the risk: To seduce a U.S. diplomat in Russia, a foreign espionage operation first sent a blond woman to his hotel room with Champagne. When he declined, the spies sent a redheaded woman, and then next a young man. The implication for OpenAI employees was this could happen to them, according to the people.

I like to think that if I was a diplomat, by the time I see the second unknown hottie show up at my hotel room with Champagne I would be pretty confident it was a trap. There are many things that are much more effective on their first try. Mix it up a little.

Kelsey Piper: I worry this makes things really hard for extremely attractive people who just want to seduce an OpenAI or Anthropic employee for their money.

Andrew Rettek: And they’re the real victims here.

Kelsey Piper: imagine being engaged in the innocent and time-honored trad pastime of marrying the richest guy you can find and being accused of international espionage just because you are really really hot.

alice: i personally want to seduce them for their extremely accurate meows

What changed is that we noticed the problem. The problem has existed for a while.

Zack Korman: The OpenAI employee who allegedly stole over a hundred confidential documents without OpenAI noticing for months sent the documents to his number *in mainland China*

This is all a big problem in its own right. If you cannot protect your secrets from spies, including the Chinese, then there is no point in trying to ‘win the race.’

This is also indicative of other problems. If you cannot solve your employee misalignment problems, how are you going to solve AI misalignment problems?

A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer

The first best way to learn with Claude is very different from ‘create practice sheets and teacher updates’ but it is a vast upgrade on similar actions without Claude.

cold: Kids these days are getting tiger parented by Claude

Jack: this rocks, in fact

I’m feeling out a Take that if a tutor is not using AI in their work at this point, they are veering towards negligence, because tutor+AI now dominates tutor alone at ~all levels of competence

Vladislav Ekimtcov: claude obsoletes school tbh. you can do an entire k-12 in a single github monorepo with fun little widgets that teach how to write every letter and add up numbers

They Took Our Jobs

Is AI changing the world? Freddie deBoer says no, ‘human life in 2026 appears to be almost entirely similar to human life in 2021.’ Jack disagrees, pointing out that all his friends and family have had their jobs transformed.

Jack: Five years of AI has changed the world dramatically more than five years of electricity or five years of the combustion engine did. It’s not even close.

AI so far has simultaneously changed the world more than any other technology (at least if you exclude military techs that won active wars) in its first five years. AI so far has also changed the world dramatically less than I or many others would have expected in that time, if we had been told the path of AI capabilities. Diffusion takes time and a lot of things have been bottlenecked.

As AI use continues to grow exponentially, expect bigger impacts, with the impact growing faster all the time, even if capabilities mostly stop improving from here.

Anthropic is hiring for a smaller share of junior positions and AI agent hours outnumber employee hours six to one. Human attention is a bottleneck for AI outputs and human productivity is way up. That’s the central finding of a new Anthropic report on what it is like to work there.

Anthropic: At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it.

… Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we’ve already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.

These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025.

They have a chart for ‘reading Claude as a full time job.’

Some think that soon either the jobs be gone or the jobs be fake.

EigenGender: There is simply no future where humans continue to do economically useful work for much longer. Your choice is at best between various flavors of “ASI let’s humans have fun and play make believe.”

(to be clear this is a good thing!)

Opinions are very strong on whether or not this would, if it happens, be a good thing. In some ways it is very good. In others it is very bad.

Anatoly Karlin: I strongly believe that everyone countersignaling against post-scarcity utopia on the basis of the “dignity” and “sanctity” of work should have do a lengthy stint as a Dhaka garments factory or African subsistence farmer. Talk is cheap from the air conditioned ivory tower.

Jack: I very strongly want a world where humans continue to pursue meaningful expertise and accomplishment, but I think Karlin is right that a lot of dignity-of-work takes come from people who have the uncommon luxury of dignified work.

Some view not having real work as being kind of AI pets (you are the pet, pejorative).

Linus Mixson: I suspect it’s as non-obvious to most people as it is to me that “ASI pets” is a more desirable future than is extinction, and I think it’s worth straightforwardly confronting the fact that Anthropic, both as a collective and at the level of its individual constituents, seems to think it rather decisively is.

Aleph: This has always seemed obviously wrong to me. If you ask the average person if they would prefer they and their family be murdered to living forever in a world of AI abundance they’re going to laugh at you. Absurd to believe otherwise.

Most talk of ‘pets for the AI’ is nonsense, but the answer to ‘does humans continuing to exist in abundance (or even adequacy) without needing to do productive work constitute a net positive future’ seems to obviously be yes. It might not be the ideal path, but the hard part is making that future have an equilibrium of that type, not coming up with net positive experiences.

Get Involved

You can go work for a Congressman on AI. Seems impactful.

Congressman Nathaniel Moran: My office is hiring an Artificial Intelligence Policy Fellow to help shape AI legislation and track AI developments in the private sector as Congress works to keep pace with the technology.

Experience in AI, policy research, or national security is encouraged.

Not AI, but if you know anyone who wants to hire Terese, she’s awesome.

Terese: I’m looking for work as a wet lab biologist in the San Francisco Bay Area. My PhD was in genetics and neuroscience but I’m open to exploring new fields. I’ve only ever been in academia, so if you do wet lab work in biotech, I’d love to hear what it’s like! DMs open.

Jakeup: I dragged my wife to SF from a post doc at a Nobel laureate’s lab at Columbia with the promise of cool Bay Area biotech. Cool Bay Area biotech, this is your chance to snap her up.

Introducing

From October 8: OSS Scanner from Anthropic, which offers free, periodic opt-in security scans for open-source projects.

In Other AI News

Utah Teapot estimates only 35k-69k people working in AI, total, from all angles.

Citrini Research goes to Anthropic’s offices to try and tell Claude to do a medical breakthrough, make no mistakes. Early results are promising and they conclude the frontier has moved, but you still have to test the ideas the old fashioned way.

Microsoft publishes a detailed report on how they did a new 3T-size pre-training. Their presentation includes chart crimes. This seems like a ‘those who know shouldn’t tell and those who tell don’t know’ style of report. Claude’s analysis is that they are still not so close to the frontier, but that this is plausibly something they can usefully license or use for recruitment, and that it has minimal uplift value.

Simons Foundation launched $15 million effort to help mathematics navigate the AI era, including contributions from Anthropic ($5 million) and OpenAI.

China is ‘cramming for the AI revolution,’ with many investing in learning to use AI. The Chinese people are (correctly) terrified of being left behind and not having a place in the future, and have a long tradition of turning to education.

FTC sends extensive civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI, as expected.

Take a minute to reflect on what the news sounds like these days, versus how sci-fi it would have sounded like two years ago. It is so easy to become numb.

j⧉nus: daily news always like dis now

Ethan Mollick wrote a book, Co-Existence, about how to live and work in a world where AI is sometimes, but not always, better than you.

Show Me the Money

Coverage of Anthropic’s financials will be in the Anthropic post later this week.

Jensen Huang is excellent at making chips, not so good at public statements.

Polymarket: JUST IN: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang assures investors the AI stock selloff is temporary, declaring, “All of this is going to pass.”

Let us say my sentiment about AI stocks did not go up hearing that sentence.

DeepSeek raises $15 billion.

Microsoft cancels UK data center deal with Nscale, in part over power concerns.

Anthropic in talks for a $45 billion cloud computing deal with Nscale. A classic your loss is our gain scenario, perhaps. Nscale is trying to IPO and lost the Microsoft project, so Anthropic should be able to press for a good deal.

NYC comptroller calls on Anthropic to pause its public offering ‘until it has fully addressed risks around artificial intelligence,’ as in permanently. He has no power over this decision, but he has thoughts.

Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case, as the judge found Meta’s deception to be intentional and did not take kindly to that. Many other states collectively settled for far less.

Trump has confirmed distribution via the Trump accounts and there is talk that OpenAI might do something similar.

SpaceX shares are trading around $146, so if all the shares are transferred Elon Musk could be granting around $10 billion. That is real money.

Giving the shares to the public sounds cool. It does not make economic sense, and the transaction costs will be high, and it does nothing to make us not die despite Musk thinking we might all die. It still might be the best option.

The reason you do it that way is symbolic, and to maybe give people the idea that they are ‘invested in’ SpaceX’s success. If that’s what gets him the motivation to do it, and how it can happen and avoid government taking a stake, then great. Second best help is still help.

Returning to Anthropic, my biggest concern is that the Benefit Fund, like many employees, will not focus on making AI go well and having everyone not die, and instead choose less impactful causes. The only action they rule out is ‘lobbying or political giving.’ Yes, offering funds to buffer against economic disruption is a noble cause, but a secondary one, and trying to fix that privately is an infinite money sink.

So how did people react to the announcement of one of the largest charitable commitments in human history (my guess is it is third but there are five all between $150 billion and $225 billion)?

Kevin Roose (out of order for dramatic effect): this post announced what could be the largest commitment of philanthropic capital ever made ($200 billion if Anthropic goes public at $1 trillion, which is probably conservative)

by my count, if Anthropic and OpenAI each go public at $1 trillion (again, probably conservative), that’s roughly $460 billion, or 5 Gates Foundations, earmarked for philanthropy-shaped things

time to start those 501c3s y’all

there’s a funny bit in the book about the Anthropic cofounders reacting to Dario asking them to pledge 80% of their equity to charity

Jack Clark considered bargaining down to 50%, but Tom Brown told him “this will either be a trillion-dollar company or a zero-dollar company”

the first reply I saw asked if Anthropic was going to use it for “gay race communism”

The replies have settled to a more reasonable place, but there is still a lot of skepticism out there about how this money gets spent. Some are more skeptical than others. It seems totally fine to reserve judgment until one sees what the money will be spent on. Someone saying ‘public good’ does not mean their spending will advance the public good.

It still seems like a telling reaction if someone pledges to give away $200 billion and your first instinct is that they are probably up to something.

Bubble, Bubble, Toil and Trouble

Current American GDP is around $32 trillion.

Kalshi: BREAKING: Anthropic says “AI could push US GDP to $44 trillion by 2030”

70% chance of IPO this year.

Elon Musk: If this is rephrased as “useful output of US”, then >50% growth by 2030 due to [AI] is extremely likely, unless there is a major war

The word ‘could’ is often used to do a lot of work. I would say that if US GDP gets to $44 trillion by 2030 and this is mostly real growth rather than inflation, then you should be freaking out rather quite a lot.

Quiet Speculations

Scott Alexander writes Against Against Handoff, as in handing off control to an aligned superintelligence or superintelligences, once such a thing is available. His central point is that all the known alternatives are worse, and your imagined ‘we will have the dumber humans in control indefinitely in the ways we need to be free to do what we want and in control, but not in a way that lets a faction of humans or AIs take over’ plan has not been properly thought out.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman lists three proposals for navigating AGI. This is a very narrow range of possible options.

Stephanie Palazzolo and Amir Efrati (The Information):

Chip City

IFP offers a big new report on chips and America’s lead over China. They conclude that America is currently six months ahead but could double this lead to a year by enforcing existing laws and using existing authority.

Tim Fist (IFP): On distillation: the current ~16x US training compute advantage would normally yield a 13-month lead. But we estimate adversarial distillation halves this to around 6.5 months.

Tim Fist, Georgia Adamson, and Konstantin Pilz (Institute for Progress): The size of the US-China AI capabilities gap is largely downstream of two factors US policymakers can influence today: China’s access to AI chips, and China’s ability to distill the capabilities of US models.

Tim Fist: The two most important interventions are:

– For BIS: Create a new end-use control to restrict China’s remote access to training clusters abroad — China’s largest and fastest-growing source of frontier-scale compute.

– For DOJ/FTC: Create a narrow safe harbor to allow US companies to coordinate on countering Chinese adversarial distillation.

Tim Fist, Georgia Adamson, and Konstantin Pilz (Institute for Progress): We estimate China’s access to AI chips will roughly double between the end of 2026 and the end of 2027. Of the portion of these chips that the US could restrict China’s access to, around half are in data centers outside China that the Chinese AI ecosystem will access remotely.

I strongly endorse cracking down on Chinese use of AI chips, as well as Chinese imports of AI chips. Even the Chinese chips that will get produced will often rely on imports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment that is a limiting factor. We should not allow that. Yes, they will build up domestic alternatives over time, but they will do that no matter what.

I also strongly endorse a safe harbor for countering distillation. The logic is similar to why safety should have such a safe harbor, except the argument is even stronger. There are competitive pressures pushing labs to not take proper defenses, and shared knowledge would be valuable.

If you are using adversarial distillation (I call it massive fraudulent distillation) to get the lead down from 13 months to 6.5 months, then both numbers matter.

  1. Chinese models available now are as good as American models 6.5 months ago.
  2. If America stopped releasing models, it would take 13 months for China to match our current best models.

My guess is that the 6.5 estimate is about right, and the 13 months is low. Notice on this chart that the 6.5 month lead is widening steadily over time, on top of 6.5 months now representing more generations than before.

If America were to maintain the current lead (6.5 months with distillation, 13 months to catch up fully) then for many purposes we will be happy to use small open models that are ‘good enough’ for quick tasks, but the frontier lead will look bigger in 2027 than it did in 2026.

If we follow IFP’s suggestions, they estimate China will only progress at half-speed in 2027, and end the year 13.1 months behind. That would be a dramatic change. A year behind still limits our options in other ways, but gives us a lot more flexibility.

For those involved in such policy discussions please read (or have your staff and AI read) the full report.

Andreessen, who voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016 and said back then that Trump’s immigration regime “makes me sick to my stomach,” explained on a podcast that he was compelled by “absolutely horrifying” discussions he once had with Biden officials. In his retelling, they divulged a top-secret plan for the federal government to take control of the AI industry and outlaw all startups and open-source software. “ ‘You guys think you can just start companies and write code and release code on the internet—those days are over,’ ” he remembered them warning in the meeting.

… The incident became Silicon Valley lore, but at first the Biden-Harris camp couldn’t even figure out what meeting Andreessen was referring to, according to four people familiar with the situation. When they finally realized he was talking about the lunch in Zients’ office, those who attended were baffled: Andreessen is prone to hyperbole, but this neared complete fiction. “It is simply false that the Biden administration told Andreessen and Horowitz that the government would ban all AI startups,” says Ben Buchanan

… As another top Biden official familiar with their visits told colleagues of Andreessen’s version of events: “Total bulls—.”

I am very happy to see Bloomberg outright call this reason crazy, because obviously that statement never happened. It did not take a firsthand account from Ben Buchanan to realize that is not a thing anyone would have said. There was never any plan remotely like this, and if there was one they would not have told Marc Andreessen about it. I spent a lot of time trying to figure out what statement got twisted into what Marc said and still today says he heard, to try and make it make sense. But no. It was always total bullshit.

The bulk of the article is a personal history, with much that is praiseworthy. They trace Marc’s transformation to after he made the most expensive home purchase in California history in Paradise Cove and became withdrawn. Andreessen’s views grew more conservative over time, or at least he increasingly disliked liberals. Then we get to the (quite bad) Techno-Optimist Manifesto in October 2023, and another complete fabrication about a particular meeting regarding AI and open source:

Austin Carr (Bloomberg.com): Andreessen recalled recently on X that Max Tegmark, an AI safety researcher at MIT, “pound[ed] the table” in front of the senators, “demanding open source AI software be made illegal.”

Tegmark says that’s totally false. Five other attendees agree, saying the closed-door meeting was cordial and uneventful; Andreessen, they remember, didn’t say much at all. It seemed to reflect a decades-long pattern of tactical fabulism.

… Four of the many a16z-backed startup founders interviewed for this story describe Andreessen’s manifesto as weirdly angry and oversimplistic.

It seems this has been a rather common strategy of Andreessen for decades, and presumably he keeps doing it because it works.

Austin Carr (Bloomberg.com): Andreessen, then at Netscape, sent his notes from a routine business meeting with Microsoft executives to the DOJ, claiming that Microsoft had explicitly threatened to annihilate his company if he didn’t cede control of the browser market. Microsoft execs who attended the meeting said they learned of these claims only years later and were bewildered, swearing that Andreessen’s recollections were nonsense.

Ultimately there is no satisfying explanation for any of it. One common sense interpretation is that, like Trump and Musk and many others, there was a death spiral of blocking out contrary views while engaging heavily with Twitter over many years. Another is that this is simply how he always did business, and the AI stuff is some combination of ideological blinders, anger at liberals and talking his book of business.

People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone

Does this mean it’s not too late?

Elon Musk: So many people are going to get one-shotted by super persuasive super intelligences and I might be one of them.

Elon Musk may have already been one-shotted by other things. So, more shots, then.

If we prepare for a natural pandemic, that ‘may not be enough’ to protect against an engineered pandemic, since the engineering can make it worse for us in various ways. Of course, we are at ‘OpenAI computer security prior to HuggingFace’ levels of operational excellence and attention for our preparation even for natural pandemics. If I had more free time I would be pushing harder on that problem.

The Lighter Side

Oh look, it’s the alignment plan.

Tenobrus: it increasingly seems like this precise plan may in fact work out for the vast majority of humanity

I mean, sure, I suppose it might work.

While you’re chilling, I guess enjoy a solid #slopcore video? Like most AI video things, there are rapidly decreasing marginal returns. You can make actually good AI videos, but those require effort and are still rare.



Discuss

item.title: The Alignment Journal: Our Approach and Related Projects
item.description:
The Alignment Journal is now open for submissions!

This is the fifth post in a series:

  • the announcement post introduced the journal's core premise and its three key innovations: paid attributed review, published review summaries,[1] and LLM-assisted workflow;
  • the features and policies post examined the shortcomings of existing venues and argued for the advantages of a journal over a conference;
  • the Adaptation to AI post described how we expect AI progress to shape the journal; and
  • the Organization, Personnel, and Scope post announced our editorial board, scope, and acceptance criteria.

In this post we go deeper: presenting our theory of change — including the status and information economics of the journal; a survey of previous related projects; and the high-level conclusions that follow from this analysis. We list some of the key performance indicators we'll track, the downside scenarios we must avoid, and possible future extensions of the journal.

The journal is being built to serve the alignment research community. This post’s purpose is to solicit feedback and encourage you to sign up on alignmentjournal.org if you want to participate. Our plans will be continually revised.

Goals

The primary function of a journal is to bring together exceptional researchers and focus their collective attention on identifying and elevating the best work. To reprise, our goals in concert with this are:

  • Improve and disseminate research on alignment that emphasizes advances in scientific and conceptual understanding.[2]
  • Combine the best features from traditional journals, ML conferences, internet forums, and social media while avoiding their pathologies: existing academic venues can be slow, opaque, myopic, and waste expert effort, while forums lack sufficient depth, filtering, and legible certification.
  • More accurately match papers to the best reviewers based on expertise and interest, making review more rigorous and carefully rationing scarce expert attention.
  • Bring researchers from traditional academia, frontier labs, and independent organizations together by providing a rigorously vetted, high-standards venue incentivizing deep contributions.
  • Filter and make legible the top alignment research results to outsiders, including to researchers in adjacent fields and to funders.

The innovations in review process, incentive design, and adaptation to AI tools are in service of the core proposition: leveraging the attention of people to accelerate progress in alignment. To that end, we must learn from the strengths and weaknesses of traditional journals, ML conferences, internet forums, and social media, drawing lessons from previous and ongoing efforts to improve academic review, as carried out by, among others, TMLR, The Unjournal, Distill, and NeurIPS.

Theory of change

The publication pipeline for academics and for AI safety researchers is ripe for disruption; there are many roadblocks to effective research that can be addressed with a well-designed intervention.

Prestige and information externalities in scholarly publication

Journals generally provide two goods: curation and public dissemination of research, and career capital for researchers. A third — belonging to and sustaining a community of peers — is important and explains a lot of why academics participate, but it complements the other two rather than competing with them, so we set it aside. The incentives governing the first two functions are potentially in conflict but can be brought into better alignment through improved institutional design.

From the perspective of the community of research users, the output of research — ideas, results, methods — is non-rival and imperfectly excludable, and its social value is maximized by broad dissemination and reuse. Research consumers need research outputs that are vetted for quality, cheap to access, easy to copy, and widely distributed.

From the perspective of the researcher, the relevant goods look different. Publication in a journal is best understood as an excludable and congestible good.[3] The journal provides ratification of one’s results, scholarly and public attention toward them, and consequent prestige and career capital. A new journal in a field that lacks one offers the prospect of generating these benefits for kinds of work that existing venues underweight. As long as the pool of researchers seeking to publish is small, these goods might be only weakly rivalrous. As the number of submissions increases, they become more strongly rivalrous. A new journal has only a limited store of attention, prestige, and career capital that it can distribute without diluting these goods by accepting work below the quality bar. Peer review and rejection are congestion control devices, intended to preserve the value of these goods.

There is therefore a presumptive tension between how journals can serve their two constituencies. Authors benefit from exclusivity which confers attention, career capital, and prestige. Readers benefit from establishing a baseline of validity but not further gating research beyond that. In the face of meager response by the dominant commercial journals to address this conflict, preprint servers have increasingly assumed a role as a demand-side solution, satisfying the distributional interests of research consumers.[4] But while the marginal cost of adding an additional reader to a digital artifact is close to zero, the marginal social benefit depends substantially on the step that preprint servers omit: validation of the research.

Separate validation from acclaim

A journal can ease this tension by separating validation from recognition. It needs to do three things. First, validate: provide the review step that preprint servers do not, and publish only work that has passed such validation. Second, distribute openly: make every published paper as cheap to access, link and cite as an arXiv preprint. Together these serve readers. They do little for authors, though. Being certified as sound earns some career capital indirectly, through the attention and impact that validation unlocks, but is unlikely to unlock the clout of acceptance in some flagship organ. The third step, then, is to supply the scarce good separately: choose a small number of the most notable of the papers already published and give them awards that bring prestige and attention.

Overlay journals already take the first two steps. They sit on top of a preprint server, run peer review, and certify accepted papers without hosting copies of their own. Some go further and add extra certifications for standout work. We plan to do all three, with a set of prizes for remarkable work at the top. If done right, these could jointly deliver the weight that publication in a highly selective journal carries in other fields.

This separation also solves a review-side problem. At a selective venue, reviewers are asked not only whether research is sound and worthwhile, but whether it deserves one of a limited number of slots: a rivalrous good that they themselves compete for, at the same time or at other times. It is unsurprising that this does not always produce constructive reviews. It is also an unreliable way to allocate acclaim, since reviewers generally do not see the field against which any given paper is competing.

Our acceptance bar is a serious one, but it is not a ranking. A paper must be correct, must advance our principled understanding, and must be the most valuable thing for at least a few researchers to read now. Each paper is judged against the bar rather than against the other submissions, so acceptance is not rivalrous in the sense above.[5] We plan to let reviewers nominate a paper for one of a small, fixed set of awards and make the case for it. Those decisions are made by a separate committee, chosen to minimize conflicts of interest, that sees the whole field of candidates. Acceptance thus signals that a paper has cleared a demanding bar, while the scarcer prestige is concentrated in the awards.

Separating validation from acclaim is not a new idea. PLOS ONE has reviewed for soundness alone since 2006, leaving importance for readers to judge after publication. eLife dropped accept/reject decisions in 2023. It now publishes reviewed preprints with an assessment that rates significance and strength of evidence on a fixed vocabulary, a cousin of our review summaries. Closest to our design, TMLR accepts papers on correctness and audience interest and recognizes significance through separate certifications. Its Outstanding certification can be awarded a year or more after publication. Its experience also points to the main risk of this approach: despite offering its own certifications, TMLR has faced a perceived “prestige gap” relative to the major ML conferences. We are betting that a more demanding acceptance bar will let acceptance carry weight in its own right, but that remains to be shown.

Remunerate reviewer labor

Peer review runs, mostly, on unpaid labor. In research communities with relatively homogeneous career objectives, review reciprocity (reviewing in exchange for being reviewed) can incentivize participation. This is common in ML conferences, e.g., ICLR, where reviewing is a condition of submitting. In alignment, many of the people best placed to review sit in commercial companies or nonprofit organizations, and may be indifferent to or actively discouraged from publication. They have nothing to get back. Reciprocity and community spirit alone are unlikely to sustain the collective epistemic enterprise of an alignment journal. We will bridge that incentive gap by paying reviewers.

Paid review has the additional advantage that payment can more straightforwardly be tied to desirable outcomes, such as review quality and insight, to avoid minimal-effort reviews that merely satisfy reciprocity conditions.

Paying for work people might have done out of goodwill can backfire. Payment can displace the motives it was meant to supplement, a risk we discussed in our features and policies post.[6] One well-known finding is that small payments can do worse than none at all (Gneezy & Rustichini 2000). This observation informs our design:

  • Payments are substantial, currently $500‒$1,700, so they read as a professional fee rather than a tip; we are explicitly valuing the work of reviewing.
  • Money is not the only reward. Reviews are attributed, and the review summary is a public, credited piece of work. Payment is an experiment we can scale back or drop if it misfires.

The evidence so far is encouraging but thin.[7] We will track review quality, invitation acceptance rates and who agrees to review, and survey reviewers on why they took part.

Desired outcomes

With these adjustments, we think that alignment research can develop a culture of peer review that it has, to date, often lacked. The requirement to pass peer review incentivizes serious engagement with existing literature, and anticipation of and engagement with objections before publication rather than after. Despite its faults, peer review can elevate the assessments of a few reviewers who deeply engage with the work rather than aggregating up many surface-level responses as is often the case on social media, especially for work that has yet to attract widespread attention. Peer review can also create new opportunities to connect work to neighboring fields.

Bringing peer review and a systematic, widely-indexed publication process to alignment research can furthermore make it more legible to prospective funders and policy makers outside of the alignment research community, who might balk at treating online forums or personal blogs as a source of research ground truth, and at relying on karma for peer review.[8]

Of course, many formal approaches to publication have led to systemic problems, such as contributing to a “publish or perish” mentality in which prestigious publications are seen as an end in themselves, instead of a means to advance a collective epistemic project. While there is no decisive way to avoid this risk, we can mitigate it by keeping acceptance a standard rather than a quota, and then allocating acclaim based not only on editor taste but on the observed usefulness of (and response to) a piece of research. The model should be prizes awarded ex post, in regular review cycles after publication, once a paper’s usefulness and reception can be observed, rather than decisions made entirely at acceptance.

Objections

We also acknowledge that online forums combined with a tightly-knit research community allow for a kind of rapid iteration and experimentation that peer review inevitably slows down. But the Alignment Journal would not seek to replace the forums and blog posts where ideas are often first worked out. Instead, it would provide a venue of record where the fully-developed versions of those ideas could be validated and distributed to the broader research community. We have prepared a downside risk pre-mortem on these and other issues.

Key performance indicators

These are some of the indicators that we will use to estimate the success of the journal, both subjective and objective. We will use these to diagnose problems, not as targets to optimize.

Who submits and reviews

  • Where authors and reviewers come from: the mix by sector (academia, frontier companies, independent) and by home discipline.
  • Do researchers submit their best research to us? “Best” is subjective of course, but conditional on whose taste you trust this is pretty measurable.

Review process (matching, rigor, speed)

  • Time between submission and publication. We expect things to start slow as we work out the kinks in the process, but our long-term goal is 1-2 months.
  • Time to first review, time in discussion and time to decision, tracked separately.[9] We want everything to go fast.
  • Review quality as rated by action editors, plus reviewers’ self-rated expertise as a check on matching.
  • Authors’ rating of how useful the reviews were, including authors of rejected papers.
  • Do people engage with, cite, and discuss the review summaries?

Legibility and prestige (outsiders, funders, career capital)

  • Article-level citations, including the share from outside the alignment community.
  • (Eventually) Impact factor and related traditional journal metrics.[10]

Downside risk pre-mortem

How could this journal have negative impact?

  • Low-quality research. We could lower the status of the field by publishing low-quality work in the “official” journal of alignment research.
  • Poor management. If we end up with “market power” but run the journal poorly, we could bring the field into disrepute and make it difficult for a better journal to get started.
  • Wrong focus. The boundaries and value of different types of alignment research are hotly disputed. We could overly reward or promote research that proves fruitless, misallocating researchers' effort and misleading outsiders on progress. Mitigation requires carefully defined criteria to make transparent decisions.
  • Narrow editorial taste becoming the field's definition of “real” alignment research. The editorial board is broad, but cannot span the whole field, and many calls are taste-based and made with limited information. Moreover, different sub-domains of alignment have differing appetites for a journal, some areas being already well-served by the flagship conferences, so we face selection bias.
  • Lack of sustainability/persistence. If we become the venue of record for important work and then lose funding or otherwise fold, our site and its contents could vanish, memory-holing the research we published. The more successful we are, the worse this would be.[11][12]
  • Publishing tools used by capabilities research. If we successfully improve academic publishing mechanisms, we could accelerate dangerous research such as the gain of offense-dominant capabilities or publish and elevate alignment work with capability externalities.
  • Waste of time. We might simply induce alignment researchers to divert some of their effort into journal activities without sufficient upside.
  • Goodharting. If awards/acclaim provided by the Alignment Journal come to have significant material benefits for recipients, we could end up incentivizing optimizing for acclaim as distinct from advancing the collective epistemic project of making powerful AI go well.
  • Reputation-washing. Frontier companies advancing AI capabilities could use the reputation and prestige of a publication in the journal to obscure harmful practices that do not live up to the standards advertised in their published work.
  • Crowding out intrinsic motivation. Paying reviewers could displace the goodwill that sustains peer review elsewhere. It could attract reviewers who are mainly there for the fee, or make unpaid reviewing in the wider field feel like a lesser obligation. We will watch review quality and the makeup of our reviewer pool, and change the payment scheme if we see either effect.
  • Funder dependence or capture. The journal’s business model depends upon philanthropic funding, thereby providing a mechanism through which the interests of funders may be imposed upon the journal. We seek to preserve our independence by relying upon a well-regarded editorial board to make decisions independently of such interests, staking reputation upon it. We welcome suggestions for further safeguards.

Extensions

If the journal is successful, it could become a good platform for several possible extensions:

  1. Replication bounties. Offer payments to third parties to do post-publication replication for certain papers that the editors judge to be notable/important and are somewhat doubted by the community.
    1. (For the time being, full replication of a paper is probably too costly, even with recent AI tools, to be done routinely, which is why we think it should not be part of the normal review process.)
    2. This is especially attractive in the light of potential sharing of expertise or infrastructure with similar organizations, e.g., The Unjournal.
  2. Public forecasts (or even prediction markets) about which publications will later achieve some objective correlate of importance or veracity, like citation count, replication, or mention in model cards or legislation. Some combination of editors, reviewers, or readers could participate.
  3. Preregistration and registered reports. We could encourage authors to preregister their hypotheses and analyses, and ask reviewers to check the paper against the registration.[13] A strong version is the Registered Reports format, now offered by over 300 journals.
  4. Retrospective review of existing published papers, either
    1. With author participation (similar to traditional peer review)
    2. Without author participation (i.e., third-party commentary)
  5. An in-person conference.
  6. Journal-to-conference track. In agreement with one or more conferences, we could “certify” some high-quality subset of papers we publish to get automatic inclusion in a track at the conferences.
    1. See TMLR’s blog post on doing this for their journal with the NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR conferences.
  7. Conference-to-journal track. Is there virtue to anointing select papers with a DOI and a seal of approval? Note that we already permit substantial expansion of conference papers.
  8. Review articles and pedagogy, perhaps commissioned, i.e., author payments. These might feature stronger editorial input and perhaps interactive content.

Appendix: Prior Art

This section contains our thoughts on a few particular existing projects related to reforming journals: Distill, the Journal of Open Source Software, the Unjournal, and Transactions on Machine Learning Research. We hope it gives a sense of how we think about these things.

Distill

Distill was a highly regarded, widely read, and unusual ML journal which focused on clear communication and pedagogy. It went on indefinite hiatus after less than five years of operations, and their post-mortem is strongly recommended reading. In our assessment, Distill had two main value-adds which, by the editors’ own assessment, were extremely labor-intensive:

  1. intense (50+ hour) mentorship to authors; and
  2. web-native interactive and dynamic visualizations.

We believe these are worthy goals, and we hope that Distill or another journal finds a way to take up this mantle again in a sustainable way; indeed, LLMs potentially greatly reduce the burden of building dynamic content. However, the primary goal of the Alignment Journal is distinct from Distill’s pedagogic goals: efficient and legible assessment of research. We will focus instead on optimizing the use of reviewer time and effort.

If the Alignment Journal overall is successful, we could imagine branching out to more pedagogical work with stronger editorial input and interactive content (among many other possibilities; see Extensions), but that would only be done with caution.

Journal of Open Source Software

The Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS) is a diamond open-access journal for research software demonstrating a wide range of innovative editorial and review strategies which have informed the Alignment Journal's thinking.

Authors submit short papers (under 1,000 words, in Markdown) and the journal reviews both the paper and the underlying code. It launched in May 2016 and by 2023 was publishing roughly one paper per day, having just hit its 2,000th paper — all with no article processing charges. For the year 2019, while publishing about 350 papers, they put their cash costs at around $800 (about $21,000 counting donated services but excluding volunteer effort from editors and reviewers).

JOSS solves a different problem — giving credit for software — than we aim to solve in the Alignment Journal. Rather than the specific details, we take from them the lesson that it is possible to do open-access peer review at scale, with a fully open-source stack, which they have done for a decade.

Automation as philosophy

JOSS automates remorselessly for cost and editor/reviewer efficiency. In practice this means proof generation from Markdown, reference DOI checking via the Crossref API, repository analysis (license detection, language detection, lines-of-code count), Crossref XML generation, DOI minting, paper hosting, reminder emails for overdue reviews, and final publication are all handled by software. The only human steps are scope decisions, reviewer matching, reading the paper, and a final proofread before acceptance.

Chatops-driven publishing

Each review takes place in its own GitHub issue, with a JOSS bot participating. Assigning reviewers, generating proofs, checking references, and accepting papers are all done by typing @editorialbot <command> in that thread. This operational pattern is called “chatops-driven publishing” by founding editor Arfon Smith. This design has several beneficial consequences:

  • New editors learn by reading existing reviews. The commands are self-documenting; you do not need a training manual, just a few completed threads to read.
  • The audit trail is complete by construction. Every state transition — reviewer assigned, checklist item checked, proof generated, acceptance triggered — is a timestamped event.
  • Operational dashboards are easy. All state lives in structured, queryable form; thus, showing editor workload, time-in-review, and bottlenecks is just a database query over existing data.

The underlying technology (a Ruby framework called Buffy deployed on GitHub Issues) does not transfer to the Alignment Journal’s needs, which require semi-confidential review, per-user access controls, and paid workflow rather than public volunteer review. But the principle seems to contain design patterns worth investigating: keep editorial tooling inside the review interface rather than in a separate system, and design every workflow around minimizing the number of clicks, context switches, and decisions an editor has to make.

Open-source infrastructure

JOSS's stack is four loosely-coupled components:

  • a Rails web app for submission intake and dashboards;
  • an editorial bot framework (Buffy);
  • a Pandoc-based document production pipeline (Inara) that produces PDF, HTML, JATS XML, Crossref XML, and CFF from Markdown source; and
  • a GitHub repository for archival storage with CI workflows for compilation and DOI deposit.

Each component can be replaced independently. Initial build cost was roughly $50K (0.25 FTE for a year). Their blog posts on cost models, scaling, and operations at 2,000 papers are worth reading for anyone designing a journal's technical infrastructure.

Where JOSS has struggled

Challenges that JOSS has faced are also worth noting for the Alignment Journal:

Review time creeps upward. Average time spent in review went from under three months (pre-COVID) to about four months by 2023. JOSS remains uncertain why; likely contributors include reviewer fatigue as the pool gets overused, submission growth without proportional reviewer growth, and the general post-COVID decline in volunteer engagement. One lesson from this is to instrument review timelines from day one, tracking time-to-first-review, time-in-discussion, and time-to-decision separately. Once a slowdown becomes visible it is much easier to diagnose where the bottleneck actually is.

Scope disputes consume disproportionate editorial time. JOSS initially handled scope questions ad hoc on a mailing list, which consumed substantial editor effort. They eventually moved to automated flagging (submissions under 1,000 lines of code get flagged, under 300 get desk-rejected), a mandatory “Statement of Need” section, and a weekly batch review of flagged submissions by the editorial team. For the Alignment Journal, scope decisions seem likely to be at least as contested. A documented, regular, low-overhead process for scope decisions from the start (rather than handling each case ad hoc) seems substantially preferable.

The Unjournal

The Unjournal offers an early-stage working example of an effort to unbundle expert evaluation from traditional journal publication. It is not itself a journal, and there are no accept/reject decisions. Instead, it overlays public evaluations (aka reviews), quantitative ratings, author responses, and manager syntheses on top of preprints and working papers, while remaining non-exclusive.[14] They focus on research with “potential for global impact” in economics, social science, policy, and forecasting rather than technical AI or ML.[15] Some aspects of their process are relevant here.

Substantive Innovations

Public evaluations/reviews/ratings, editorial synthesis

The Unjournal publishes the full “evaluation packages” with DOIs for every research object they consider. This creates a rich public artifact for later readers, funders, and policy makers, and it makes the labor of review legible instead of discarding it after an editorial decision. We're unlikely to fully go down this route: our journal still uses optionally-confidential referee reports and editorial selection. However, our proposed review summaries are motivated by a similar goal: reviewer attention should produce something more informative than a one-bit accept/reject, and a summary of those findings should be prepared with the reader in mind. Their “prize-winning evaluations” provide some strong examples of value add by creating a richer signal.

Structured evaluation and quantified ratings 

As The Unjournal does not use an accept/reject filter, they emphasize quantitative ratings and predictions as a measure of research prestige and credibility. We're unlikely to ask for this level of structured rating for a typical publication, although we plan to give a small number of awards.

Prioritizing impact, links to impact-focused practitioners and stakeholders

The Unjournal's field specialist teams explicitly prioritize research for its potential real-world impact (along the lines discussed here). They also actively engage funders and practitioners as stakeholders, particularly through their Pivotal Questions projects and workshops. The Alignment Journal's editorial team might also consider impact in editorial selection and triage, and could take steps toward making evaluations legible to the broader alignment ecosystem, including companies, funders, and governance bodies.

Procedural innovations and tools

Compensating reviewers

The Unjournal pays evaluators (see their current policies), including promptness incentives and substantial cash prizes for the strongest evaluations. Their rationale cites evidence that financial incentives shorten turnaround times. The Alignment Journal plans a similar approach, paying reviewers and editors where existing norms leave their work under-incentivized and unpaid. Neither organization has yet published data on how payment affects reviews; we intend to.

Publisher-independent hosting and editorial management tools

The Unjournal has explored and adapted a stack of tools and platforms for managing their processes (research prioritization, identifying expertise, managing review, etc.), hosting their output, integrating it with the scholarly/bibliometric ecosystem (DOIs etc.), and engaging academics and practitioners. Their tools are generally linked to the open-access journal, open science, and “publish, review, curate” initiatives and communities. They are increasingly moving toward structured automations and code and database solutions, facilitated by AI coding tools.

Automation and the use of LLM tools to enhance reviewer/evaluator work

The Unjournal is exploring the use of LLMs to enhance evaluator work, including automated auditing of quantitative claims and structured checklists.[16] Their emerging policy requires evaluators to stand by any content in their report as their own judgment, and to disclose how AI tools were used, ideally providing links to chats or explanations. We share this general orientation: the goal is to build systems that facilitate responsible AI use and transparent reporting.

Transactions on Machine Learning Research

In machine learning, conferences are the journals. This is background knowledge for ML practitioners, but can be surprising to other scientists. The venues of record are a few giant annual conferences — chiefly NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR — not journals. A paper accepted there is peer-reviewed, archival, citable, and is what counts for hiring and tenure. Thus there is a single fixed annual deadline per venue (so tens of thousands of papers arrive at once), review compressed into a few intense weeks by reviewers who just submitted their own work, and accept/reject decisions with only a short rebuttal and little of the revise-and-resubmit dialogue normal in a journal. Acceptance is gated on novelty and impact rather than mere correctness. Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR) was built as a response to various strains upon this system.

Its parent journal, JMLR, was itself a protest. JMLR was founded in 2000 by MIT's Leslie Pack Kaelbling to make ML research free to read on the web, at a time when the field's main journal, Kluwer's Machine Learning, was paywalled and retained copyright control of submitted articles. In 2001 Michael I. Jordan coordinated a mass resignation — roughly 39–40 editors, about two-thirds of the board — who redirected their effort to JMLR. JMLR is now an umbrella covering the PMLR proceedings series, the MLOSS software track, and TMLR.

TMLR was announced on 12 December 2021 by inaugural Editors-in-Chief Hugo Larochelle, Raia Hadsell, and Kyunghyun Cho, with funding from CIFAR, Mila, the Vector Institute, and DeepMind. The founders cited the challenges of the conference system as motivation: “disenchantment with the exclusivity of our top conferences,” “slow turnaround,” “high-stakes pressure and stress around a handful of fixed deadlines,” and a perceived decline in the quality of the peer review process at the flagship conferences. TMLR is an overtly experimental solution, positioned somewhere between the conferences and original-flavor JMLR in its design choices. Peer review is conducted on OpenReview rather than JMLR's in-house system. And unlike JMLR, TMLR does not accept extended versions of previously published conference papers.

Design decisions:

  • Acceptance is based on correctness, not novelty or impact. TMLR’s acceptance criteria reduce the whole accept/reject decision to a handful of questions: (1) are the paper's claims “supported by accurate and convincing evidence”?, (2a) would “some individuals in TMLR’s audience be interested in the findings of this paper”, and (2b) does the paper communicate them clearly? Novelty, significance, and impact are explicitly not criteria, and reviewers are forbidden from rejecting on those grounds; authors whose claims overreach are asked to add evidence or “adjust (reduce) their claims” to fit what they have shown. A correct, modestly-scoped result is publishable on its merits.
  • Significance is judged separately. Significance judgments are made in optional, rarely-awarded certifications — Outstanding (≈ best-paper, ~once a year), Featured (≈ oral/spotlight), plus Reproducibility, Survey, and a journal-to-conference (J2C) certification that lets ~10% of accepted papers be featured at NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR.
  • Rolling submission with no deadlines; each paper runs on its own timeline.
  • Fast turnaround backed by capped workload. Reviews are due within 2 weeks (4 for submissions over 12 pages) and decisions are targeted for ~9 weeks after submission, supported by a reviewer cap of roughly one paper at a time and ~6 reviews a year. Practical turnarounds can be longer and TMLR “does not make any guarantees.”
  • Per-paper action editors (equivalent to conference area chairs) who own a paper end to end, and a fully open review process on OpenReview.

Operational record and open tensions. TMLR’s annual reports put its median time from submission to decision for conference-length papers at about three months. It was 76 days in its first year (2022 report), and 91 days in both 2023 and 2025 (2025 report). That is faster than NeurIPS (126 days from deadline to notification in 2025) but no faster than ICML (about 91). TMLR has held that pace while submissions grew from about 100 a month in 2023 to about 250 in 2025, and they roughly tripled again in the year to mid-2026. The strain shows. The editors report that they “repeatedly run low on reviewers throughout the year”, and their median is well above the 60–70 days it would take if everyone met their deadlines.

Questions remain about the career value of TMLR papers. Because a plain acceptance deliberately says nothing about significance, commentators note a “perceived prestige gap,” and early-career researchers are “incentivized to shoot for conference papers above all else”, i.e., not TMLR. TMLR’s 2023 survey is more encouraging but self-selected. About three-fifths of submitters rated its accepted papers comparable to those at NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR, a fifth rated them better and a fifth worse. Reviewers and action editors were less positive. TMLR has sought conventional markers of standing: it obtained Scopus indexing in 2025 because “at certain institutions, publishing in journals indexed by these services is an important component for career advancement.”

The subjectivity of the acceptance criteria is still debated: once novelty and impact are removed, the second acceptance question — “would some individuals in TMLR's audience be interested in the findings?” — is subjective. This is phrased permissively — some individuals, not many, and with no judgment of how interested — so a rejection on this ground has to argue that essentially nobody would care, which is far harder to sustain than a conference reviewer's familiar “not novel enough.”

Lessons for the Alignment Journal

We share some features with TMLR: rolling submission, acceptance that does not necessarily demand strict novelty, and significance signaled separately through rare certifications, some awarded after publication. We depart from it on our acceptance questions. TMLR asks only whether some readers would be interested, a threshold most sound papers meet: in 2025 it accepted 70.6% of submissions, excluding withdrawals and desk rejections (2025 report). Our Value criterion asks instead whether a paper is the most valuable thing for at least some alignment researchers to read now, which is somewhat narrower. This makes acceptance itself a stronger signal, at the cost of a harder and more subjective judgment for reviewers, so we are wading back into a more delicate trade-off, which TMLR chose to avoid. Whether this is the correct posture remains to be seen.
